claims.text: In situ heating in an aberration-corrected TEM/STEM combined with EDS/EELS can investigate the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles at atomic scale.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are near-equiatomic.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are approximately 5–10 nm in diameter.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have homogeneous compositions.
The proposed experiment heats the nanoparticles stepwise from room temperature to approximately 1000 °C while acquiring TEM/STEM images and EDS/EELS maps.
The proposed heating environment is high vacuum or inert gas, with temperature increments of about 100 °C and stabilization at each step.
TEM/STEM measurements can directly track compositional heterogeneity, faceting, agglomeration, and morphological changes at atomic scale during heating.
Near-equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will exhibit minimal elemental segregation at elevated temperatures.
Near-equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will exhibit minimal coarsening at elevated temperatures.
High configurational entropy in AuCoCuNiPt suppresses the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation.
Suppression of phase separation by configurational entropy reduces elemental segregation in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Configurational-entropy effects reduce growth or coarsening of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles at elevated temperature.
AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will retain a predominantly uniform elemental distribution with little phase separation during heating.
AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles tolerate higher temperatures than simpler binary or ternary nanoalloys before substantial segregation or coarsening occurs.
Binary or ternary nanoalloys lacking comparable entropic stabilization exhibit recognizable coarsening and segregation under equivalent heating conditions.
Temperatures above approximately 1000 °C or prolonged exposure may overcome the proposed entropic advantage and cause significant coarsening and phase segregation.
Prior high-temperature data for quinary Au-based high-entropy nanoparticles are limited, and their upper stability limit is not well defined.
Segregation, phase separation, or rapid coalescence significantly below 800 °C, or no retardation relative to simpler-alloy controls, is defined as a falsifying outcome.
